title: Surfaces of revolution
section: Analytic Geometry of R3 ▷ Surfaces of Revolution
terms: surface of revolution; axis of revolution; radial distance; ellipsoid of revolution.

exposition.text:
A surface of revolution is obtained by rotating a plane curve about a line in its plane. Rotation

2 2
about the z-axis preserves z and the distance x + y from the axis; rotation about the x-axis
√
2 2
preserves x and y + z .

If the curve z = f(x) in the xz-plane rotates about the x-axis, the result is y + z = f(x) , with
the original restrictions on x. More general implicit equations require considering both possible
signs of the radial coordinate. Squaring can introduce unwanted branches, so retain restrictions
such as nonnegative heights or a limited generating interval.
An ellipsoid of revolution is an ellipsoid with two equal semiaxes, obtained by rotating an el-
2 2 2 2 2
lipse about one of its axes. About the z-axis its equation is (x + y )/a + z /c = 1. The
equal semiaxes a are perpendicular to the rotation axis, while c is along it. For a translated
axis, measure radial distance from that line rather than from the coordinate axis.

question.text:
The segment z = 2 − x, 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, in the xz-plane is revolved about the z-axis. Which describes
the resulting surface?
2 2 2 2 2
(A) z = 2 − x − y (B) x + y = (2 − z) , 0 ≤ z ≤ 2
2 2 2 2 2 2
(C) x + y = z (D) x + z = (2 − y)
2 2 2
(E) x + y + z = 4

solution.text:
The distance to the z-axis equals the original nonnegative x = 2−z, and the original segment
√
2 2
implies 0 ≤ z ≤ 2. Thus x + y = 2 − z.
